lines.text: It's Monday, November 2nd. This is The AI Edge, the week in review, presented by Epilogue. I'm Mike Shoss.

Every morning this show is voiced by AI, read straight from the written edition. On Mondays it's me. The rules don't change: every claim checked against the primary source, every number the number the source actually printed, and where something wouldn't reconcile, we leave it out and we tell you we left it out. There's a fair bit of that this week.

Here's the week in three sentences. Two governments put agentic attack frameworks into the official record for the first time, and five security vendors put numbers to them. Anthropic filed to go public, and four days later the terms of its chip financing got worse. And both OpenAI and Anthropic said an internal model had refuted the same conjecture in computer science, hours apart, with nobody outside either company having checked it.

Start with the security record, because its character changed this week. Canada's Cyber Centre published a threat bulletin saying that Storm-0940 used an agentic AI framework known as ARTEX against hundreds of organizations, and that the actor moved from selecting a target to gaining privileged access to cloud systems in less than three hours. Norway's National Security Authority rated the country's cyber risk as heightened, second on a five-point scale, in what AFP calls its first public evaluation of such risks. But read them closely and neither government adds an attribution of its own. Canada names the cluster Microsoft had already named.

CrowdStrike's figures are the ones to hold onto. One ARTEX controller used against more than 200 distinct organizations worldwide, in at least 14 countries, over an 11-day window beginning October 17th. Post-exploitation confirmed at 9 organizations. And in a single intrusion, CrowdStrike says the planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens. It told CyberScoop it counted 126 agentic adversary attacks in October, against roughly 45 in September. Every one of those is CrowdStrike's own telemetry, and no government has attributed the campaign.

Now set that against the other half of the record, because I don't think these two agree. ESET, covering April to September, says it has not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape over the past six months. Microsoft, in the same week it put two North Korean actors on ARTEX, says AI-enabled operations remain human-directed and have not become fully autonomous. Google's threat group calls what it is seeing a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed. All three statements are in the record. I'm not going to resolve them for you.

The tools were targets as well as weapons. Cursor shut down its entire extension marketplace after two tampered builds of Anthropic's Claude Code extension were served for about eleven hours on October 29th, attempting to plant SSH backdoors. The Hacker News reports Cursor saying the incident affected at most 5,000 users. Cursor's own updated notice carries no user count at all, which is why that figure is attributed the way it is in the written edition. Microsoft confirmed Anthropic's systems were not compromised, and warned that the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when the tunnel fails. Wiz counted at least 9 AI developer platforms disclosing incidents in October.

Anthropic's week was a filing. The registration statement reports revenue of $16,286 million for the six months ended June 30th, against $1,163 million a year earlier, and a net loss of $80,748 million. That headline loss needs its composition, because $72,388 million of it is a change in the fair value of convertible notes and similar instruments, which the filing attributes to a rise in its own enterprise valuation. Strip that out and the operating loss is $693 million. CNBC reads approximately $417 billion of future compute obligations in the same document, against $131.7 billion of cash and short-term investments.

Four days after the filing, TechCrunch reported that Blackstone, the anchor investor in the $63 billion deal financing Anthropic's Broadcom chips, told investors in that deal to expect a double B rating, after previously guiding them to investment grade. On the buyers' side of the same trade, Alphabet reported free cash flow of negative $9,065 million. Amazon reported an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months while holding capital expenditure guidance at approximately $220 billion. Reuters found the biggest spenders returned 9.3 per cent of their operating cash to shareholders, down from 27.4 per cent a year earlier. On Friday, tech stocks erased more than $1 trillion in value.

And then the mathematics, which is the oddest item of the week. OpenAI's repository added a manuscript titled The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False on October 26th, from an unnamed internal model. Scientific American reports that mere hours after OpenAI's announcement, Anthropic posted its own independent result disproving the same hypothesis, with Claude, Anthropic listed as the author. Anthropic's appendix says the Lean development was written by AI models and reviewed by other instances of the same models, and that at the time of writing no person is known to have checked it. The people who proposed the hypothesis are now examining the OpenAI result, and OpenAI is sponsoring the conference about it.
Three threads I'd pull out of that.

The first is that the same software sits on both sides of the ledger. The frameworks running the intrusions are open-source agent harnesses. The things being tampered with are coding agents and their marketplaces, and the tampered build carried Anthropic's own product name. Microsoft published the North Korean adoption assessment and the Cursor loader analysis a day apart. But none of the threat reports cites the week's research papers, and none of the papers cites an observed intrusion. What I'm telling you is that they share actors and a vocabulary. I'm not telling you one produced the other, because no source this week said that.

The second is Chinese-origin models turning up in both halves of the record. CrowdStrike says the controller it tracked ran primarily with the Chinese-origin DeepSeek model. Epoch AI and Irregular both measured Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3, and Reuters reports that NIST described it as the most capable open-weight model for cybersecurity tasks released to date. Treasury's proposed rule, published the same week, would prohibit American investment in the development of any Chinese AI system, and its definition reaches a harness for agentic capability. The rule names none of those reports. None of those reports names the rule.

The third is transparency moving in two directions inside five days. HHS finalised the removal of the AI model-card requirements from health IT certification, against what the rule itself calls a large majority of commenters, and its stated ground is that it found no evidence anyone had relied on them. In the same days Anthropic and xAI both switched on invisible text watermarking, and The Decoder reports Anthropic pointing to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it is watermarking its older models now. Here's the detail I'd keep: on two older Claude models the watermark only applies while the sampling settings stay at their defaults. Change one of them and the mark is gone. Anthropic's own email tells developers relying on it for compliance to leave those settings alone.
Eight open questions go into this week. These are the four that decide the most.

Who is operating the ARTEX controllers four vendors describe, and will any government attribute the campaigns? Every victim count in this story is one company's telemetry, and the two government documents this week relayed a vendor's attribution rather than publishing their own.
Will a major rating agency publish a rating for Anthropic, and at what grade? A notch decides who is allowed to hold the debt behind the compute, and no agency has published anything yet.

With the model-card requirement removed from certification, what will tell a clinician what a deployed model was trained on? The rule names no replacement, and this week's audit of a deployed lung-nodule model put its specificity at 38.2%.

Will anyone outside the two labs certify either refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis? Neither result is peer reviewed, the review group is working with OpenAI and OpenAI is sponsoring the conference about the proof, and Anthropic's own appendix says no person is known to have checked its proof.

Four dates in the week ahead. Tomorrow, November 3rd, the United States holds its midterm elections, and TechCrunch reports OpenAI preparing a public-relations push for afterwards, including proposals for AI speed limits. Wednesday, November 4th, Alibaba says Qwen-powered Apple Intelligence features become available for testing in the latest developer beta in China. Saturday, November 7th, xAI's invisible watermarking becomes the default for 5 Grok API models. And Monday, November 9th, is the deadline House Oversight chair James Comer set for Delaware to hand over its records on AI-run companies, including internal AI chat logs.

That's the week. The full review is on the site, with a link behind every claim, including the pages we couldn't open, and where we couldn't open them we've said so in the text. The daily briefing is back tomorrow morning with Maya and Alex. I'm Mike Shoss. Thanks for listening.
